summary_en: Do people care more about inequality at home or across countries, and what shapes those attitudes? Cervone, Gáspár and co-authors run a 31-country representative survey and find that concern about cross-country inequality is widespread but systematically lower than concern about within-country inequality, even when respondents see themselves as relatively poor in global terms. Concern correlates with perceived deservingness of poorer countries and with respondents' own political identity, not just their own income rank.
data_used: A representative cross-country survey covering 31 countries, with stylized-fact summary of attitudes toward cross-country and within-country inequality and respondents' own perceived position both nationally and globally.
policy_relevance: Useful for Hungarian and EU debate on development-aid budgets, EU cohesion-fund flows, and migration-policy framing: the paper shows that 'global poverty' arguments are politically weaker than 'national inequality' arguments and that perceived deservingness moderates support. For Hungarian public-opinion strategy on EU funds and ODA, framing transfers in terms of within-country inequality is likely to be more effective than appeals to cross-country fairness.
title: Inequality Perception and Preferences Globally and Locally
